title: How do you know a spider is asleep?
hook: A motionless spider might simply be waiting. Two behavioral tests help tell the difference.
paper_title: Behavioral evidence for two-stage sleep in spiders
summary: Laboratory jumping spiders showed characteristic rest, REM-like movements, reduced responses to sound and a rebound in REM-like time after disturbance.
evidence_note: Behavioral evidence, not proof of dreaming or direct neural equivalence; distinct arousal groups of 10 and paired rebound sample of 13.

evidence.design: Distinct laboratory behavioral assays; detailed sleep architecture n=10; arousal n=30 (10 per state, separate animals, single trial); sleep disruption 17 tested and 13 paired analyzable.

claims.claim: Rest posture with recurring twitching and retinal movements.
claims.location: Main Results sleep behavior, Methods and Figures 2 and 5.

claims.claim: Responders during REM-like bouts responded more slowly than awake responders; four of ten REM-like animals did not respond within 10 seconds, all four later responded awake.
claims.location: Main Methods arousal threshold, Results and Figure 3.

claims.claim: Thirteen analyzable paired spiders showed more REM-like bouts and total REM-like minutes after fly disturbance (9.4 to 16.9 minutes).
claims.location: Main Methods sleep disruption and Results rebound, Figure 4.

limitations: Quiet wakefulness may occur within sleep windows.
Distinct arousal groups; responding-only latency estimate; REM-like versus quiescent comparison not significant after adjustment.
Disturbance is not demonstrated complete deprivation; no continuous recording of the disturbance night.
No direct neural measurement or evidence of dreams.
All values are main-text group summaries; no supplementary footage or individual traces used.

segments.speech: At night, a jumping spider stops moving. Is that sleep, or just waiting?
Researchers looked for more than stillness. On silk platforms, the spiders adopted a resting posture.
Rest was interrupted by bouts of twitching and movement of their retinal tubes.
Then came a sound test. Among spiders that responded, reactions during REM-like bouts were slower than when awake.
Four out of ten in those bouts did not react within ten seconds. They reacted when retested awake.
captions: in those bouts did not react

segments.speech: Next, researchers disturbed a night with fruit flies. This interrupted sleep, not necessarily all sleep.
Thirteen spiders had usable before and after recordings. They showed more REM-like bouts and more total REM-like time.
That supports regulated sleep with REM-like periods. Brain activity was not measured. This does not show that spiders dream.

posts.caption:
A motionless spider might just be waiting. In laboratory Portia fimbriata, researchers looked at rest posture, twitching, retinal movements, responses to sound and rebound after a disturbed night. Four of ten spiders tested during REM-like bouts did not react within ten seconds, but reacted when awake. Thirteen paired recordings showed mean REM-like time rising from 9.4 to 16.9 minutes after fly disturbance. Behavioral evidence supports sleep with REM-like periods, not proof of dreaming or direct neural equivalence.

Geiger et al. (2026), PNAS. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2618030123
Full text: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13752372/
Evidence and credits: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/sources/tt-011.html
Photo: Donald Hobern, CC BY 2.0, species reference only. Original conceptual animations; synthetic neural narration.
